claims.text: Phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by the interplay between valence electron concentration and local atomic strain.
Increasing VEC beyond a critical threshold while holding atomic-size mismatch constant destabilizes the fcc phase in favor of the bcc phase.
Increasing the bcc fraction will enhance high-temperature strength.
Increasing the bcc fraction will enhance radiation tolerance.
Increasing the bcc fraction will maintain or enhance cryogenic toughness.
Conventionally processed Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni can have a predominantly fcc or mixed fcc+bcc initial microstructure.
A minor substitution using a higher-VEC element of similar atomic radius can increase overall VEC without appreciably changing atomic-size mismatch.
The relative Gibbs free energies of fcc and bcc phases govern their thermodynamic phase stability and can be used to realize an fcc-to-bcc transformation.
Increasing VEC electronically lowers the free-energy difference between competing fcc and bcc phases.
Crossing a critical VEC threshold promotes bcc formation by destabilizing fcc.
The fcc-to-bcc phase transition mediates improvements in high-temperature strength and radiation tolerance.
The proposed VEC-driven mechanism remains valid across high-temperature, irradiation, and cryogenic testing regimes when atomic-size mismatch is controlled.
Large lattice distortions can dominate phase stability and invalidate the proposed VEC-based relationship.
Temperature and other processing or microstructural factors may influence phase stability and the resulting outcomes.
